readings.c1s3:
¶
'''4.''' To change the position or posture of the body, as in bed; shift or roll from one side to the other.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''turn’d'' and try’d each corner of my bed,
To find if sleep were there, but sleep was lost.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''5.''' To change direction; take an opposite or different course or way.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then shalt thou see the dew-bedabbled wretch
''Turn,'' and re-''turn,'' indenting with the way.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 704.}}}}

'''6.''' Specifically, to put about; tack.
{{smaller block|He spy’d a Dutch Sloop ''turning'' to get into the Road, and saw her at the evening Anchor at the West end of the Island. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 52.}}}}

'''7.''' To change one’s attitude or policy; hence, to rebel; offer resistance; show fight: often with ''upon'': as, to ''turn upon'' one’s accuser. See ''to turn on'' (''a''), below.
{{smaller block|Should I ''turn upon'' the true prince?
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 297.}}
<poem>Even the instinctive worm on which we tread
''Turns,'' though it would not.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Julian and Maddalo.}}}}

'''8.''' To retrace one’s steps; go or come back; return.
{{smaller block|<poem>Either thou wilt die, by God’s just ordinance,
Ere from this war thou ''turn'' a conqueror,
Or I with grief and extreme age shall perish,
And never look upon thy face again.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 184.}}}}

'''9.''' To retreat; run away; also, to desert; go over to the enemy. [Rare.]

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|turn|6539|turn}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|He strewed the City . . . with salt, having first ''turned up'' the ground with a plough. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 131.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') To bring or put a different surface or side uppermost; place with the face upward: as, to ''turn up'' a card.}}

{{smaller block|Your lordship is the most patient man in loss, the most coldest that ever ''turned up'' ace. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 3. 2.}}}}

{{smaller|(''c'') To give an upward turn or direction to; bring the end, tip, or point of uppermost; tilt up: as, to ''turn up'' one’s nose (an expression of contempt).}}

{{smaller block|Her deuotion at the Church is much in the ''turning vp'' of her eye, and turning downe the leafe in her Booke when shee heares nam’d Chapter and Verse.
{{right|''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, A Shee Precise Hypocrite.}}}}

{{smaller|(''d'') To refer to in a book: as, to ''turn up'' a passage or text.—'''To turn upon''' (or '''on'''), to direct or cause to operate upon or against; hence, to cast back upon; retort: as, he ''turned'' his sword ''upon'' himself; to ''turn'' the arguments of an opponent ''upon'' himself.—'''To turn up one’s toes,''' to die. [Slang.]—'''Turned commas,''' reversed commas (“), used in marking the beginning of a quotation, and under a word or words to indicate repetition.—'''Turning-off machine,''' in ''stocking-manuf.'', a machine for closing the seam in stockings which have been knit flat. ''E. H. Knight.''}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To have a revolving or rolling motion; move round, as on an axis, pivot, or hinge; revolve.

{{smaller block|He that is giddy thinks the world ''turns'' round.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., v. 2. 20.}}}}

{{smaller block|If it [a cannon-ball] should strike any part of the body when the velocity . . . is greatly diminished, it does not carry it away, . . . but, in consequence of its circular or rolling motion, it ''turns'' round the part, in the same manner as a wheel passes over a limb.
{{right|''J. M. Carnochan'', Operative Surgery, p. 134.}}}}

Hence — '''2.''' Figuratively, to move as on a point of support; hinge; depend: with ''on'' or ''upon'': as, the question ''turns upon'' this point.

{{smaller block|The Chorus ought to ''turn upon'' the Argument of the Drama, and support the Design of the Acts.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 149.}}}}
{{smaller block|Great events often ''turn upon'' very small circumstances.
{{right|''Swift'', Conduct of Allies.}}}}
{{smaller block|A playfulness that ''turned on'' her supposed oddity was not at all to Maggie’s taste.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, ii. 1.}}}}

'''3.''' To move so as to face in a different direction or in some specified direction; direct one’s face, course, efforts, attentions, thoughts, etc. (in some particular direction): as, to ''turn'' toward Mecca in prayer; to ''turn'' down a shady lane; I know not which way to ''turn.''
{{smaller block|<poem>At thys present time of it speke no more,
Vnto my purpos ''torn'' shall I therfore.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 518.}}}}
{{smaller block|Abjure this magic, ''turn'' to God again.
{{right|''Marlowe'', Doctor Faustus, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I know not where to ''turn''. O, welcome home!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 1. 197.}}}}
{{smaller block|Trust me, Sir, I thought we had wanted three miles of this house; . . . now we are at it, we’ll ''turn'' into it, and refresh ourselves with a cup of drink.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 56.}}}}
{{smaller block|Just within the Gate, we ''turned'' up a Street on the left hand, and were conducted by the Consul to his own house.
{{right|''Maundrell'', Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Great souls by instinct to each other ''turn'',
Demand alliance, and in friendship burn.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', The Campaign.}}}}
{{smaller block|There is no Point of the Compass to which they cannot ''turn'', and by which they are not turn’d.
{{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, ii. 6.}}}}

'''4.''' To change the position or posture of the body, as in bed; shift or roll from one side to the other.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''turn’d'' and try’d each corner of my bed,
To find if sleep were there, but sleep was lost.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''5.''' To change direction; take an opposite or different course or way.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then shalt thou see the dew-bedabbled wretch
''Turn,'' and re-''turn,'' indenting with the way.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 704.}}}}

'''6.''' Specifically, to put about; tack.
{{smaller block|He spy’d a Dutch Sloop ''turning'' to get into the Road, and saw her at the evening Anchor at the West end of the Island. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 52.}}}}

'''7.''' To change one’s attitude or policy; hence, to rebel; offer resistance; show fight: often with ''upon'': as, to ''turn upon'' one’s accuser. See ''to turn on'' (''a''), below.
{{smaller block|Should I ''turn upon'' the true prince?
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 297.}}
<poem>Even the instinctive worm on which we tread
''Turns,'' though it would not.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Julian and Maddalo.}}}}

'''8.''' To retrace one’s steps; go or come back; return.
{{smaller block|<poem>Either thou wilt die, by God’s just ordinance,
Ere from this war thou ''turn'' a conqueror,
Or I with grief and extreme age shall perish,
And never look upon thy face again.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 184.}}}}

'''9.''' To retreat; run away; also, to desert; go over to the enemy. [Rare.]
<poem>Whan thi haf o’ thi Gordones desertit,
An’ ''turnit'' wi’ Murray in a crack.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Battle of Corichie'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 213).}}}}

'''10.''' To change or become altered in nature, character, quality, appearance, or the like; be converted, transformed, or transmuted; hence, in general, to become; grow: as, to ''turn'' gray; to ''turn'' pale.

{{smaller block|He that kepeth it clanly a yere, aftre that yere, hyt ''turneth'' yn to Flesche and Bloode.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 124.}}
Thy mirth shall ''turn'' to moan.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 3. 44.}}
<poem>All the happiness
Bestow’d upon me ''turns'' into disgrace.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iii. 1.}}
<poem>Why how now eyes? what now? what ’s heere to do?
I’me gone, or I shall straite ''turne'' baby to.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', Woman Killed with Kindness (Works, [ed. 1874, II. 150).}}
That every one who ''turned'' Christian was sure by that means to forfeit the favour of his prince, and to be looked upon as an apostate from the religion of his country.
{{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. iii.}}
Their design was to ''turn'' pirates, and plunder the Spaniards.
{{right|''Swift'', Gulliver’s Travels, iv. 1.}}
You’re a nice article, to ''turn'' sulky on first coming home!
{{right|''Dickens'', Martin Chuzzlewit, xxvi.}}
One of them asked her when her hair had begun to ''turn''.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVII. 135.}}}}
{{smaller|In particular—(''a'') To shift.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now all this Scene shall to Arcadia ''turn'',
The Seat of happy Nymphs and Swains.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', Semele, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To change from a fresh or sweet condition; become sour or spoiled, as milk or cider.}}

{{smaller block|Cow-milk thus prepared I judge to be better for a consumption than ass-milk, which . . . ''turneth'' not so easily, but is a little harsh. {{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 51.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') To become light, dizzy, or giddy, as the head or brain; reel; hence, to become distracted, demented, or mad.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll look no more,
Lest my brain ''turn.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 6. 23.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller|(''d'') To become nauseated, qualmish, sick, or disgusted, as the stomach. (''e'') To become inclined in another direction. (''f'') To change from ebb to flow or from flow to ebb, as the tide.}}
{{smaller block|The tide ''turned'', and rushed as fiercely in the opposite direction. {{right|''Macaulay'', Von Ranke’s Hist. Popes.}}}}
'''11.''' To be changeable, fickle, or inconstant; vacillate.
{{smaller block|She bade love last, and yet she fell a-''turning.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Passionate Pilgrim, l. 100.}}}}
'''12.''' To tend; result: with ''to''.
{{smaller block|I asked if he was unwilling to be made knowne to some greate man, for that I believed it might ''turn to'' his profit. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Jan. 18, 1671.}}

Of late the West India coffee, which is not so good, has sold so cheap that it does not ''turn to'' account to send it to England. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 134.}}}}
'''13.''' To take form on the lathe; undergo the process of turning on a lathe: as, ivory ''turns'' well.—'''To turn about''', {{smaller|to turn the face in another direction; wheel or face about: as, he ''turned about'' and faced me.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O think na ye my heart was wae,
When I ''turn’d about'', away to gae?</poem>{{right|''The Lament of the Border Widow'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 87).}}}}
'''To turn again.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To return.}}
{{smaller block|Oure Lady cam to hem, and bad hem ''tournen aȝen.'' {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 61.}}}}

{{smaller block|Therefore, O ye children of Israell, ''turne agayne'', like as ye haue exceaded in your goinge backe.
{{right|''Bible of'' 1551, Isa. xxxi. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His big manly voice,
''Turning again'' toward childish treble.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7. 162.}}}}
(''b'') To make a stand and face the enemy; turn on an enemy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Can honour pull the wings of fearful cowards,
And make ’em ''turn again'' like tigers?</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iii. 3.}}}}
'''To turn against''', to rebel against; become unfriendly or hostile to: as, my friends have all ''turned against'' me.—'''To turn aside.''' (''a'') To leave a straight course; go off in a different direction.
{{smaller block|I have therefore ''turned aside'' from that beaten path, and chosen though a less easy yet a more profitable way.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, i. 16.}}}}
(''b'') To withdraw from the presence or the notice of others; avert the face: as, to ''turn aside'' to hide one’s blushes.—'''To turn away.''' (''a'') To leave a straight or usual course; deviate; depart.
{{smaller block|When the righteous ''turneth away'' from his righteousness, . . . shall he live?
{{right|Ezek. xviii. 24.}}}}
(''b'') To turn the face in another direction; avert one’s looks.
{{smaller block|She paused, she ''turned away'', she hung her head.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}
'''To turn back''', to go or come back; return.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Turn back'' to me,
And play the mother’s part.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxliii.}}}}
'''To turn in.''' (''a'') To bend or point inward: as, his toes ''turn in''. (''b'') To enter.
{{smaller block|''Turn in'', I pray you, into your servant’s house.
{{right|Gen. xix. 2.}} <poem>Take ye that, my hireman chiel,
And ''turn in'' here and dine.</poem>
{{right|''The Hireman Chiel'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 235).}}
There is nothing so interesting as one of these Oriental cafés, and so I ''turned in'' from the street, drew a square straw-covered stool up to a low table, and held up one finger.
{{right|''The Century'', XLII. 77.}}}}
(''c'') To go to bed. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|I mean to toss a can, and remember my sweetheart, afore I ''turn in''.
{{right|''Congreve'', Love for Love, iii. 15.}}
No man can be a sailor, or know what sailors are, unless he has lived in the forecastle with them — ''turned in'' and out with them, and eaten from the common kid.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 57.}}}}
(''d'') To turn about. — '''To turn off''', to deviate from a course; be diverted: as, the road ''turns off'' to the right. — '''To turn on''' or '''upon'''. (''a'') To show anger, resentment, or hostility toward; confront in a hostile or angry manner.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Turn on'' the bloody hounds with heads of steel.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iv. 2. 51.}}
Pompey ''turned upon'' him again, and in effect bade him be quiet.
{{right|''Bacon'', Friendship.}}}}
(''b'') See def. 2. — '''To turn out'''. (''a'') To bend or point outward: as, her toes ''turn out''. (''b'') To come abroad; assemble out of doors; muster: as, the volunteers ''turned out'' in force; the people ''turned out'' to see the show.
{{smaller block|Then from every house and hamlet the men ''turned out''.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Backlog Studies, p. 125.}}}}
(''c'') Specifically, of workmen, to abandon work in order to go on strike.
{{smaller block|“What do you say to a strike, by way of something pleasant to talk about?” “Have the hands actually ''turned out?''” asked Mrs. Thornton.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', North and South, xviii.}}}}
(''d'') To get out of bed; rise. [Colloq.] (''e'') To prove in the result or issue; appear or show in the end; terminate; result: as, the affair ''turned out'' better than was expected.

{{smaller block|That you have a wealthy uncle I have heard; but how your expectations will ''turn out'' is more, I believe, than you can tell.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|I never had a wife, but I have had two or three broomstick matches, though they never ''turned out'' happy.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 353.}}}}
'''To turn over''', to move, shift, or change from side to side, or from top to bottom: as, to ''turn over'' in bed.—'''To turn round.''' (''a'') To turn so as to face the other way; reverse one’s position. (''b'') To reverse one’s opinions or relations; go over to another side or party: as, he ''turned round'' and voted with the Whigs.—'''To turn rusty.''' See ''rusty''<sup>3</sup>.—'''To turn to.''' (''a'') [''To'', prep.] (1) To be directed toward: as, the needle ''turns to'' the pole. (2) To tend to; result or terminate in. Compare def. 12. (3) To apply one’s self to; betake one’s self to; direct one’s efforts or attention to; resort to.
{{smaller block|<poem>What is that which I should ''turn to'', lighting upon days like these?
Every door is barr’d with gold, and opens but to golden keys.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}
(''b'') [''To'', adv.] To begin operations; set to work.
{{smaller block|I found that no time was allowed for day-dreaming, but that we must ''turn to'' at the first light.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 8.}}}}
'''To turn Turk.''' See ''Turk''.—'''To turn under''', to be bent, doubled, or folded downward or under.—'''To turn up.''' (''a'') To point upward: as, her nose ''turns up'' slightly. (''b'') To come to the surface; hence, to come to light; appear; happen; occur: as, to be waiting for something to ''turn up''.
{{smaller block|Those accidental visitations of fortune are like prizes in the lottery, which must not be put into the year’s income till they ''turn up''.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', To John Allen, Jan. 24, 1813.}}}}
{{smaller block|“And then,” said Mr. Micawber, . . . “I shall, please Heaven, begin to be beforehand with the world, . . . if—in short, if anything ''turns up''.”
{{right|''Dickens'', David Copperfield, xi.}}}}

{{smaller block|If after three thousand years a black swan ''turns up'', must we not suppose it possible that in three thousand years more we may see a candle burn in an atmosphere of pure nitrogen?
{{right|''J. Fiske'', Cosmic Philos., I. 54.}}}}

{{smaller|(''c'') To turn belly upward: said of a dying whale.}}

'''turn''' (tėrn), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''tourn'', ''tourne'', ''torn''; < ME. ''turn'', ''tourn'', ''torn'', < OF. ''tourn'', ''tour'', a turn, trick, round, etc., F. ''tour'', a round, travel, tour, etc.; from the verb. Cf. ''tour''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Movement about a center; circular motion; rotation; revolution: as, the ''turn'' of a wheel; a ''turn'' of the wrist.
{{smaller block|His Passion is Metamorphos’d in the ''Turn'' of a hand.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 227.}}
<poem>A gallant daunce, that liuely doth bewray
A spirit and a vertue masculine, . . .
With lofty ''turnes'' and capriols in the ayre.</poem>
{{right|''Sir J. Davies'', Dancing.}}}}
'''2.''' A turning into another or a different way; a change of movement or direction; a deviation; also, the point at which such a change of course is made.
{{smaller block|True Repentance is the ''turn'' of the whole Soul from the Love as well as the Practice of Sin.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, III. i.}}
When one sees the beggars and the commonplace and shabby condition of Spanish Granada, . . . he may perhaps give a new ''turn'' to his reflections by visiting Tetuan.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Roundabout Journey, p. 181.}}}}
{{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Change to an opposite direction, or the point at which such change is effected: as, the ''turn'' of the tide. (''b'') Deviation from a straight-line course or direction; bend; curve; flexure; angle: as, a ''turn'' in the road cut off the view.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
